#1313. AI’s energy paradox: will the AI boom strain energy systems or be the source of solutions?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Melissa Hobson is a freelance marine-science journalist based in Hastings, UK.

Ginelle Greene-Dewasmes is working to make AI energy use more sustainable.

Artificial intelligence is exploding in popularity, and many people have concerns about the sustainability of its energy consumption. AI models need vast amounts of electricity: according to the International Energy Agency, a typical AI data centre can consume as much energy as 100,000 households each year. Energy use by US data-centre servers more than tripled between 2014 and 2023 — reaching 4.4% of the nation’s total electricity consumption. This figure is expected to at least double by 20281.

However, AI might also hold the key to improving energy efficiency: offsetting some of the demand it creates. An article published by the World Economic Forum suggests that the use of AI tools across industries — in automating tasks or monitoring real-time energy use, for example — can reduce energy consumption by up to 60%. Ginelle Greene-Dewasmes, a sustainable-development specialist and an author of the article, has been working to lower AI’s energy demands while finding ways to use the tools to reduce wider emissions.

Originally from Trinidad, Greene-Dewasmes became interested in solving energy-security issues for island states with few resources. In 2021, she completed a PhD on the green-energy transition across small island developing states at the University of York, UK, before joining the World Economic Forum in 2022. Now based in Geneva, Switzerland, Greene-Dewasmes has been the Forum’s AI and Energy Lead since 2024. Her work involves bringing together AI and energy leaders from around the world to identify shared challenges, align priorities and develop practical actions that can improve AI’s energy impact.

As well as looking at improving AI’s energy efficiency, Greene-Dewasmes and partners are exploring how models can find innovations that improve existing energy infrastructure, such as that in buildings that are already in use. Nature spoke to her about navigating the increasing energy needs of the technology and whether its benefits could outweigh this demand.

AI needs cloud networks, chips, graphics-processing units and cooling systems, all of which consume large amounts of energy. Developing and training models requires high levels of processing power to crunch the data, but AI use is much more energy intensive overall because of the scale. ChatGPT, the chatbot from technology firm OpenAI in San Francisco, California, has more than 800 million users each month and receives more than 2.5 billion queries daily. As AI becomes mainstream, we need to build more energy infrastructure to keep up with the surge in demand.

But, when it comes to scaling up AI, I think the conversation is too skewed towards the energy needed to power centralized infrastructure, when there are lots of other things that will contribute to AI’s energy requirements. Large data centres will exist in only the few countries that have the money, space and resources to host them. For most of the world, AI infrastructure will be disaggregated and decentralized. For example, if one million people are using their phones more intensively because of AI, that affects the energy infrastructure.

Although more complex LLM queries are currently directed to remote data centres, some smaller tasks can be completed directly on new devices that have AI chips. As this becomes more common, what will that mean for infrastructure planning for energy? It’s much harder to measure this than the outputs from one data centre.

AI’s electricity impact is currently about 0.49% of total global electricity use — so it’s still fairly small, although it’s growing. The World Economic Forum, in collaboration with other specialists, has created a Net-Positive AI Energy Framework. It looks at how we can design AI models and infrastructure for efficiency — by optimizing chips, data-centre locations and liquid cooling, in which fluids are used for cooling owing to their high heat capacity — while using AI to bring down energy usage in high-impact sectors, such as transportation and urbanization, both by improving the efficiency of systems and coming up with solutions to global challenges.

For example, in Azerbaijan, operations that keep buildings running, including lighting, heating and cooling, account for a large proportion of the country’s carbon emissions. The Centre for the Fourth Industrial Revolution Azerbaijan (a public legal entity) is using AI-powered solutions to improve efficiencies as part of its nationally determined contribution commitments — the country’s pledge to reduce emissions. This includes AI solutions that adjust heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) on the basis of building occupancy and use trends, and that predict the need for maintenance before faults arise. In some cases, this use of AI to hone efficiency has brought down HVAC energy use by 25% and emissions by up to 40%.

We’re also encouraging people to use AI wisely. We want AI to reduce energy consumption overall, rather than adding strain to systems.

The aim is to gather insights from leading voices in the AI ecosystem to generate thought leadership and encourage cross-discipline learning so people aren’t working in silos. It started off as one-on-one conversations with professionals working with AI, centred on the technology’s biggest challenges and opportunities. We convened a community of about 40 people, which has increased to around 70 in nine industries around the world and is still growing. We try to hear from lots of voices: university academics, public-sector entities and technology, AI and energy companies (including renewables and nuclear) are all involved. Together with our partners, we turn these insights into guidance and frameworks that can support the wider industry.

We’ve published two reports based on the learnings gleaned from these thought leaders. Artificial Intelligence Energy Paradox explores how to balance the challenges and opportunities of AI and energy. The Net-Positive AI Energy Framework is our North Star for clean, efficient and equitable AI. We’re now working on an AI Energy Readiness Compass: a methodology to support responsible AI energy developments and identify the causes of upcoming bottlenecks in the power grid that could be problematic for AI energy use.

One particular success from these collaborations is the willingness of hyperscalers — large organizations that operate cloud computing services and data centres — to embrace grid flexibility. At first, they were reluctant to adjust when they draw power because they wanted continuous access to reliable electricity, but they have come to see the benefits of balancing demand on the grid. As a result, they have embraced power flexibility, and 18 partners supported the launch of the AI Energy Management Alliance: a coalition of companies that promotes dynamic load-shifting (changing when energy is used to align with grid loads, the availability of green energy and the best pricing).

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03412-5

#1311. Harry Kane proves there is only one Ballon d’Or winner

Let’s cut to the chase. If there is any justice, sanity or logic in football then Harry Kane will win the Ballon d’Or when the ceremony takes place in London on Monday.

Arsenal would have deservedly won this Champions League match away to Bayern Munich if Kane was not on the pitch. Instead, they almost lost it but for another bit of brilliance from Declan Rice, Kane’s vice-captain for England, and probably his successor to wear the armband.

A brilliantly worked team-goal finished off by Declan Rice, and Arsenal are level 💥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/Y25zI80A0z

“I’m lucky I can play with him and not so lucky I have to play against him,” Rice said, and that summed it up succinctly.

And that Ballon d’Or? There is bias, but Rice – who is also on the 30-strong list of nominees – added of Kane: “He is the clear winner. His numbers speak for themselves, the year he has had has been remarkable. When you play with him you realise how good he is and when you play against him you see how much of a pain it is.”

Arsenal stood toe-to-toe with Bayern in an open match. Both sides went for it, partly because they knew under the Champions League format, that defeat was not a disaster. There has been some chat about whether Arsenal can be, well, a bit dull. Not here. It would be no surprise to see these two face off again deep into this competition.

The only setback for Arsenal was a worrying injury to Bukayo Saka early on, limping off and tapping his thigh, indicating an issue with his muscle. Mikel Arteta’s reaction betrayed his understandable concern.

Kane won a penalty and then expertly took it to give Bayern the lead. Other strikers could have scored the penalty but few would have created the wonderful assist that drew Bayern level.

It has been a fact for quite some years that Kane is not only the best goalscorer for England but the best passer. Indeed, if Kane could provide for Kane he would have scored even more goals.

“Unsere nummer neun,” shouted the stadium announcer after Kane’s goal and that needed no translation. Kane is a god in Bavaria, where they know a few things about having great centre-forwards. But the 33-year-old is surpassing them all.

Kane’s goal meant he had scored in 10 straight Champions League games, one short of the record held by Cristiano Ronaldo. It was also the former Tottenham Hotspur forward’s 16th goal in 23 games against Arsenal. No one has ever scored more against them.

Kane is the complete player, carrying out his defensive duties – winning headers to clear Bayern’s lines from Arsenal free-kicks – to linking the play to being the focus of his team’s attacks. He is a centre-half, central midfielder and centre-forward. Who pops up on the wing to deliver pinpoint crosses.

Maybe Kane will be pipped at the Palladium – the theatre where the ceremony takes place – by Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal or Real Madrid’s Kylian Mbappé, or even an absurd sympathy vote for Lionel Messi. But Kane deserves it. His time is now.

Some passages of play in the first half deserve analysis. Just to highlight how good Kane was. After an Arsenal corner, wastefully volleyed over by Riccardo Calafiori, Bayern countered and suddenly it was three on two. Serge Gnabry, the former Arsenal winger, had to do better than shoot weakly when picked out on the overlap. David Raya saved. That was a let-off.

But who sprung that counter? It was not Manuel Neuer, the Bayern goalkeeper, taking the goal-kick, but Kane, with his sharp thinking. And then Kane launched a superb pass from deep which Ismael Saibari should have dealt with better. It should have been another opportunity. Potentially a goal.

Is there anything Harry Kane can't do? 🧐 His goal kick very nearly led to a Bayern Munich goal 😲 https://t.co/fqbsN7KOjw

And then Bayern did score. The ball was played inside to Kane, in centre field and afforded too much space. He delivered a perfectly weighted through ball for Alphonse Davies to run on to. The pace was perfect, allowing the Canadian not to break stride and stroke it past Raya. Kane did not fire the ball in, he did not make Davies work to reach it and he did not give Jurrien Timber any chance of cutting it out. It was perfect. Some excellent, if disquieting, detail from Sam Dean in this piece about the mood around Arsenal away from the first-team following the news of 60 planned redundancies. Sam writes that there are expecting to be other experienced and influential figures departing. The timing of cuts invites particular scrutiny, coming after the emotional peak of winning the league, record revenues and Mikel Arteta’s new contract.

After Arsenal were beaten by Bayern Munich in a Champions League quarter-final two years ago, Mikel Arteta bemoaned a lack of “magic moments” in attack.

Arsenal have since progressed to a Champions League semi-final and final, while ending a 22-year wait for a Premier League title.

The upward trajectory has translated to tangible success, but Arsenal are still searching the level-raising attacker they lacked on their last visit to the Allianz Arena in 2024.

Back then, Arsenal’s offensive game revolved around Kai Havertz, Bukayo Saka and Martin Odegaard and that remains the case, which makes one wonder if Arsenal’s forward options have been adequately renewed.

A pair of stodgy performances (in victory) against Leeds United and Nottingham Forest have amplified those questions, though some of Arsenal’s slicker football in the season’s early weeks has been forgotten a little hastily.

They have made another strong start to another European campaign with six points from six, but this is undoubtedly their hardest fixture of the league phase.

Their chances of matching last season’s eight wins from eight could well hinge on the outcome of tonight’s game, but there are worse times to face Bayern.

Vincent Kompany’s team looks as formidable as ever, having scored 22 goals from six Bundesliga games so far this season. Their rotational approach is hard to track, with runners from deep breaking beyond Harry Kane who wanders into deep midfield positions.

However, they are without Michael Olise (suspension) and Jamal Musiala (injury) while Joshua Kimmich will miss the game on compassionate grounds following the death of his father.

With the exception of William Saliba, Christos Tzolis and Piero Hincacpie, Arsenal have a pretty clean bill of health and the strength of their bench was crucial against Leeds, Lille and Forest last week.

For Arteta, there are some interesting selection calls to make. It is anticipated that Jurrien Timber will replace Ben White at right-back, and first-choice left-back Riccardo Calafiori has been rested for the Champions League games so far. Should Arteta continue that policy, Myles Lewis-Skelly will fill the position, which will likely mean a midfield start for Bruno Guimarães or Mikel Merino.

Arsenal’s manager must also decide between Noni Madueke and Eberechi Eze on the left, and Viktor Gyokeres and Kai Havertz up front. Havertz is Arteta’s preference, but he also has to consider a relatively short turnaround before Saturday’s league game against Everton.

Manchester City and England midfielder Rico Lewis has revealed that he sees midfield as his preferred position, while admitting that securing regular first-team football is his biggest priority as he looks to return to England’s senior squad under Thomas Tuchel.

Speaking exclusively to GIVEMESPORT reporter Sam Cohen during the England Under-21s’ November international camp in Bristol, Lewis discussed the challenges of competing for minutes, the influence of Pep Guardiola, his memories of Manchester City’s historic treble, and the next generation of England talent.

Having played at right-back and in midfield during 122 appearances for Man City, Lewis explained how his view of his best position has developed over time.

The 21-year-old said: “It’s been interesting. I’ve enjoyed playing wherever, but now I’m kind of getting that feeling where I enjoy helping the team going forward.”

“So I think the best place to do that is in the midfield for me. Finding that joy of scoring, assisting, that’s what’s kind of driving me to that feeling.”

He was equally clear that versatility remains an asset: “It’s nice to play any time. It’s not like I only want to play here and I can’t play anywhere else, because it’s a positive thing to be able to play in different positions as well.”

Lewis has senior England experiences under his belt with five caps to his name, and believes that he can bring those experiences and responsibility when playing alongside his teammates in the Under-21s.

“I’ve got my experience of being here already and with the seniors. I think in terms of on the pitch and off the pitch, standards and making sure I’m driving them as much as I can with the other players that have been here for a while as well.”

He added: “What you do off the pitch will most likely leak onto the pitch, good or bad. So if it’s good off the pitch, then there’s no excuse for it to not be good on the pitch as well, and vice versa.”

Asked about getting back into Tuchel’s senior squad, Lewis linked that ambition to his club minutes. “I definitely appreciate all the help that comes with the England structure in general. But for me, it kind of links to what we said about the goal in 12 months’ time, is playing as many games as I can.”

“The more minutes I play, the more I can show what I can do and the more that puts me in good stead to get selected. But I think I’m just focusing on just working as hard as I can right now to get into that position to play and then from there it all snowballs.”

Lewis spoke openly about staying mentally ready when appearances are hard to come by.

“There’s so much competition that when you get your opportunity you have to take it.

“Preparing myself mentally, not playing, not playing, not playing, then getting the chance to play, there’s no point in wasting that 90 minutes wishing I was playing those other games I’m playing right now.”

He said that accepting the ups and downs of football ultimately makes a player stronger.

Looking 12 months ahead, his priority is straightforward: “For me it would be literally playing as many games as I can do ... having that experience of playing sustained minutes and consistently.”

Rather than a specific statistical target, he wants to feel that he is playing, learning, growing and improving.

Asked what he took from Guardiola and how he was adjusting to a different managerial approach, Lewis stressed the belief that powered City’s success.

“Obviously Pep was very demanding and rightfully so. I think that’s the way you win things.”

“The togetherness of the team and the belief in the system and the belief that we’re going to win. I think that’s greater than any tactic, going into every game thinking we’re going to win this game, we’re better than the other team.”

Lewis added: “You can take that with you wherever you go, instead of a tactic or a system. If you have that personal belief or team belief that you’re going to go and win, I think that’s stronger than anything else.”

When asked about the moments that made him realise what he had achieved, Lewis immediately chose his Champions League goal against Sevilla.

“That’s a moment where, even after it happened, I was like, 'I can’t believe this happened.'” He admitted he had watched it back “so many times”.

But the whole experience of entering the City dressing room as a teenager was just as extraordinary.

“Even just being around them in training and being in that dressing room over a whole year when I was 17 turning 18, the whole experience was…” He agreed that it felt like a dream. “You don’t really take it in. And now I can look back and say I understand what was actually going on.”

Could those famous personalities be overwhelming? “Yeah, it can do,” Lewis said. “They’re not just top players, they’re top people. So that definitely helped me integrate into the team and feel more comfortable.”

He nevertheless acknowledged that even with support, the quality around him could feel overwhelming.

Lewis was part of Manchester City’s historic 2022/23 treble-winning squad. He said the magnitude of the achievement can still be difficult to absorb.

“There’s not many players in the world who walk around and say they’ve won a treble.

“Life goes so fast that you don’t really have time to think about it. But sometimes I do think and I think how lucky I was to be in that team.”

He thanked Guardiola, one of the best managers in world football, for giving him his opportunity: “Obviously I worked hard ... but I’m grateful to Pep for giving me the opportunity to be part of that and to be in a dressing room when one of the best seasons in world football was going on.”

Lewis expects that perspective to deepen with time. “I think in ten years’ time I’ll look back and say I didn’t even realise how amazing it was to be in that treble winning team.”

Asked who had stood out in the England Under-21 camp, Lewis praised the collective level before naming Liverpool youngster Trey Nyoni.

“All the players are top, high-level players ... I think Trey has been good this week in training. But all the players have been good.”

The Young Lions are preparing to face Portugal and France at Ashton Gate in Bristol as part of their build-up to next summer’s Under-21 European Championship.

The interview ended with ten rapid-fire football questions.

Who is the best player you trained with? Kevin De Bruyne.

Who is the toughest opponent you have faced? Vinicius Junior.

Who is the funniest England Under-21 player? Ethan [Nwaneri] or [Alfie] Devine

What would be your position for life? Midfield.

What is the best stadium you have played in? The old Camp Nou

What skill would you like to master? A showboating skill such as a scissor, or a step-over.

Who is your first England Under-21 five-a-side selection? Ethan [Nwaneri]

Which player would you most like to play alongside (other than Messi or Ronaldo)? Kaka. I’d like to get a Kaká shirt.

Despite a remarkable collection of early career experiences, Lewis’s central message was consistent: more minutes, more opportunities to develop, and the chance to push back into England’s senior squad.

His explicit preference for midfield offers a revealing glimpse of where he sees his future, while his memories of Guardiola and the treble underline how much those formative years continue to shape him.

#1309. Former Old Firm rivals reveal how clubs walked a fine line between rivalry and respect...and even stopped by for tea and sympathy in times of trouble!

Published: 12:20 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 12:29 EST, 13 November 2026

They have reached an age when they would once have been categorised as the old infirm. Yet in the autumn of 2026 they cavort around Toryglen with an almost juvenile vigour.

They have reached the age when they can reflect on being stalwarts of the Old Firm. Yet they are outlining plans and strategy for a vital, growing movement.

The two meetings are separated by two sets of stairs. On the ground level, men of pensionable age and beyond play walking football. Just above sit Campbell Ogilvie, former secretary of Rangers and president of the Scottish FA, and Eric Riley, once company secretary and director of Celtic.

They are both on the board of Walking Football Scotland, an organisation that now has more than 5,000 people playing the game across 160 clubs, with participants ranging from 40 to 93.

The venerable statesmen of the Scottish game may be perceived to be rivals, but only in matters on the pitch. They sit in an office in the south side of Glasgow and reminisce about how they first met 50 years ago when playing five-a-sides and then renewed that rivalry in their professional life.

As the Glasgow rivals now seem regularly at odds, both men recalled a time when friendship was paramount amid the sporting mayhem.

Former Rangers secretary Campbell Ogilvie and ex-Celtic director Eric Riley are firm friends

‘The two clubs always had a good relationship back in those days,’ said Ogilvie, now 76 and still playing football. ‘We wanted to beat each other — naturally. But off the field we had a very close relationship.’

He told a remarkable story that backs that assertion.

‘There was one day I was at Ibrox in the early 1980s when the team was not doing so well. The phone rang and it was Sean Fallon, Jock Stein’s former Celtic assistant. I had known Sean from my days with the Scottish League and he said: “I know you’re going through a rocky spell, so I’m coming over for a cup of tea”.

‘Over he comes. So there was a very close relationship in those days. I’m not there now and for all I know there still is. But certainly, when I was there and Eric was at Celtic, we could talk to each other.’

Riley, 69, agreed: ‘Absolutely. John McClelland (former Rangers chairman) was one we could talk to. And Martin (Bain, former chief executive) I suppose, when he came along a bit later. Between myself and Peter Lawwell (former Celtic chief executive and chairman) the relationship between the clubs off the field was actually quite strong. But on the field we still wanted to win.’

Ogilvie added: ‘There was a respect. And I go back to the Willie Waddells and the Willie Thorntons, there was that respect. More recently that was there with the likes of Jack McGinn and so on.

‘We had a good relationship but it’s fair to say that there was no social media in those days. You know all the toxic stuff that can bring.’

The traits of respect and sporting competitiveness have been obvious in both men since they first met half a century ago. ‘We played five-a-side football at Scotstoun before the football careers started. It was just casual games,’ said Ogilvie. ‘We were in our early 20s. Eric was an accountant and I think those games were arranged through accountants.

‘I played youth football when I was 16 and, 60 years down the line, playing football is still a major part of my life.’

Ogilvie began walking football eight years ago and Riley soon after. ‘I suffer from Parkinson’s, amongst other things,’ said Riley. ‘I was getting assistance through Stobhill Hospital and the physiotherapist there, who specialises in Parkinson’s patients, got in touch to say there was a project going on at Toryglen where they were playing walking football and assessing you to see what the benefits may or may not be.’

Ogilvie and Riley are both on the board of Walking Football and have played a big role in its rise

Riley agreed to take part. ‘I really enjoyed it because you are back playing football again, you have the camaraderie and you have the home baking which I never really get at home.’

Riley had a hip replacement in March and admitted: ‘I have not played since then. I miss it. I play a few other things which are more and more difficult. I play tennis.’

His tennis history is illustrious as he played with Judy Murray in Scottish championships. ‘She went off to the tour and I went off to university,’ says Riley. He is unstinting in his praise of the woman who became the mother of the No1 in men’s singles and men’s doubles.

The repartee between Riley and Ogilvie is relaxed but both men have a resolve to grow walking football. Their task has been helped by bookmakers William Hill stepping in with sponsorship.

The benefits of the sport stretch beyond the physical. Ogilvie gave his own experience.

‘When you have finished working, there is a void, not mixing with people, not being with people, and walking football certainly has helped me fill that. Hopefully it helps me keep a bit fitter too,’ he said.

Ogilvie pointed out: ‘The issues you tend to encounter are health. Grief is another one. There are quite a few of the guys who have lost their wives and quite a few who are just sitting on the sofa watching Homes Under the Hammer.’

Walking football, too, has attracted a large cadre of women. ‘One of the things that stood out for me was the number of females playing,’ said Riley. ‘I went along to my first session and there were four female players, three of whom had never kicked a football in their life previously. Walking football got them involved and they really enjoyed it.’

Walking football has made giant leaps in Scotland but the next step is to collate data so cases for funding will be made unanswerable.

‘We need facts or what is called data,’ said Ogilvie. ‘We are trying to do some studies with universities to get that data — physical and mental — and get it to the government. We want to prove the benefits and then we could make this prescriptive through surgeries.

‘We see the benefits day to day anecdotally but that doesn’t bring you the data. Sponsorship helps.

Walking Football attracts thousands of participants at clubs across the country

‘The university studies won’t come overnight because they need to be detailed. But if we could get to the stage where we could prove the benefits, then the NHS and the government would see that proof in black and white.’

This is all serious and proper. But both men were keen to emphasise that the game was fun. Ogilvie said: ‘When I started, I asked someone: “How would you sum up walking football?” He said to me: “It’s a cross between watching Barcelona and the Gurkha warriors”.’

He added: ‘I loved when at the end of an over-75s tournament one player said to another: “Good game, son”.’

The football world has thus moved into a new era. But some things cannot change. Ogilvie said: ‘One of my grandsons, who is 10, came along to watch a session and said two things. Firstly, it is a bit more intense than he thought and second there are no pink boots.’

Riley chimed in: ‘That would be an affront, that would be unacceptable.’

Even in walking football some things are a step too far.

■ Eric Riley and Campbell Ogilvie were speaking at the announcement of William Hill as official sponsor of Walking Football Scotland. To find your nearest game visit walkingfootballscotland.org

#1308. Tare: ‘Milan biggest disappointment was Pulisic, choosing Allegri, Cardinale problem’

Milan sacked Igli Tare in May, but he has broken his silence on why he chose Max Allegri, not getting the chance to speak to owner Gerry Cardinale, and why ‘Christian Pulisic was the biggest disappointment.’

The former Lazio chief was brought in as director of sport, a role that until his arrival had not existed at the club for a while, since the dismissal of Paolo Maldini and Ricky Massara in 2023.

He did not even last a full year, as Tare was sacked along with coach Allegri, CEO Giorgio Furlani and director Geoffrey Moncada with a single, brutal press statement on May 25.

“The wound of failing to qualify for the Champions League is still deep, enormous in fact,” Tare told Sky Sport Italia Calcio Unplugged.

“If I come to a club like Milan with the target of getting into the Champions League, then I don’t know where I am. This is the most successful club in Italian football history, and after Real Madrid it is the most important in the world.”

RedBird patron Cardinale had been an aloof figure at first, but decided after cleaning house that he would take a much more hands-on approach to running the club.

“I am disappointed that those leading the club didn’t understand people needed to be given time, something that they are now doing better,” added Tare.

“I’d say you need several transfer market sessions to get a team that is competitive and ready to win. At the start, there was an important responsibility, missing out on Europe altogether and losing the Coppa Italia Final did a lot of damage to morale.

“We sold players for a lot of money and signed 10 new figures, so it takes time to integrate, understand and create a united group. We had, albeit in difficult circumstances, been first or second up until the end of March and start of April. In the last 10 rounds, our mentality just collapsed due to other issues that I don’t want to get into, but they did have an effect.

“I admit we too deserve some of the blame, because Max and I should’ve paid more attention to certain dynamics, be more present with the squad to get the season over the line.”

When Tare was brought in, it was meant to be as a director of sport, but he insists he never had a direct line to the man with the purse strings.

“I remember when we were in negotiations for Ardon Jashari, he called and wanted to understand what was happening. He said ‘if you need to spend a little more, just let me know, and I’m ready.’ However, I never got the chance to speak with him directly again, because there were people above me I didn’t want to over-ride.

“It would’ve been helpful to everyone, not just me, if we’d been able to discuss it directly. I think this is a new experience for Cardinale, he is used to other sports in America, but now he has taken on the responsibility at Milan.

“I would’ve preferred to have that presence when I was still at Milan, as it would’ve been very useful, but better late than never for the good of the club. I think the good of Milan is top of his priorities too.”

Among the roles tasked to Tare was the choice of a new coach, and he plumped for Allegri.

“I was thinking of the experience he brought at that time. When I arrived, the only thing I was asked was to hire an Italian coach, not a foreign one,” revealed Tare.

“I had a few ideas for foreign coaches, but the experience with Sergio Conceicao and Paulo Fonseca evidently wasn’t what they were after. Allegri won a lot as a coach, Milan is special to him, he won the Scudetto there first, so of course he was sad at the way it ended.

“He is not alone, Zlatan Ibrahimovic and Alessandro Nesta had great experiences elsewhere too, but Milan stands out for them, and I can confirm it’s true.”

This is also a legendary club abroad, and it is what prompted the arrival of Ballon d’Or winner Luka Modric as a free agent after the experience at Real Madrid.

“I had the sensation this squad lacked leadership. The idea along with Modric was to sign Granit Xhaka, who at the time was the captain of Bayer Leverkusen, to guide the others. Luka is more silent in his attitude on the pitch.”

There was an intriguing comment from Tare that suggested more tension behind the scenes with some players.

“The biggest disappointment was Pulisic, I expected more from him in terms of responsibility and leadership. He’s a great player, but some things happened that I had never experienced in my career. Pulisic didn’t score a goal for six months. Santiago Gimenez didn’t score either.

“I guess these things happen in football, but when you have a drought that long, it ends up affecting the whole team’s performance.”

#1307. Mauricio Pochettino's Most-Used Players at Every Team

From Espanyol days all the way to his biggest task yet at Manchester United, Mauricio Pochettino boasts one of the most interesting portfolios in world football. The Argentinian has even taken charge of the US Men's National Team, reaching the last 16 in their home World Cup in 2026.

His biggest achievements came at Tottenham Hotspur, however, even if silverware never reflected that. From a struggling, inconsistent side, Pochettino took the Lilywhites all the way to the Champions League final, where they fell at the final hurdle against Liverpool. His legacy remained intact nonetheless, as was the case when he took charge of London rivals Chelsea.

Poch's side became so successful because of his modern, high-intensity ideas. In many ways, he was the Andoni Iraola of the Premier League before Iraoal, himself, stepped foot in England, and Man United will be desperate to benefit next.

But who might the new manager trust the most? Historically speaking, he's often leant on some surprising names.

Pochettino's love affair with attacking midfielders started in the exact same place that his management career got underway. At Espanyol, it was Joan Verdu who took centre-stage, as the Argentinian's side battled to stay afloat in La Liga.

The attacking star enjoyed some of the best form of his career under Pochettino's guidance, scoring 19 goals and assisting another 18 in 131 games in all competitions. Only Jordi Vinyals managed to drag a bette record out of the Spaniard, who showed the early signs of what Pochettino can do with attacking players.

He wasn't the only one to benefit, though. Luis Garcia - another attacking midfielder and centre-back Juan Forlin were also mainstays under the South American at Espanyol.

Pochettino's most used players at Espanyol

Make no mistake about it, Pochettino has always prioritised finding attacking stars who he can trust. And that will be music to the ears of Bryan Mbeumo, Benjamin Sesko and Matheus Cunha, three of Man United's recent transfer signings.

After Espanyol, Pochettino took the Premier League by storm at Southampton, taking the Saints to as high as eigth in the 2013/14 campaign.

Once again, an attacking player took his most-trusted role, with Rickie Lambert playing more games than anyone else at St Mary's during the manager's reign as the then-Southampton boss sought-out a clinical striker who could hold the ball up for midfield runners.

The forward didn't disappoint either, scoring 19 goals and assisting another 12 in just 55 games under Poch. Together with the likes of Morgan Schneiderlin, Lamert was crucial.

Pochettino's most used players at Southampton

Just like it was Verdu at Espanyol, Pochettino's most-used player at Tottenham was an attacking midfielder in Christian Eriksen. The Dane became a cult hero at Spurs during the Argentine's reign, putting himself among the best creators that the Premier League had to offer at the time.

As Harry Kane commenced the long journey towards eventual Ballon d'Or stardom in 2026 by stealing the show at Spurs, Eriksen's role was crucial. And Pochettino knew it. By the time the pair split off, the former Spurs man had scored and assisted a combined 133 goals in 55 games.

"Christian is doing, in my few years, always an important player for us. He always steps up and I think he's this type of player who represents our philosophy."

In many ways, Eriksen was the orchestrator behind Pochettino's Spurs greatness. If Man United are to have any success, then they must find a player who can replicate the midfielder's quality under the former Tottenham manager.

Pochettino's most used players at Tottenham

The Premier League is dominated by a few teams, leaving some of the country's biggest clubs to never win it.

The PSG spell will arguably the most disappointing of Pochettino's career. On paper, he had everything that a manager could ask for. He had the ultimate trio of attacking stars in Lionel Messi, Kylian Mbappe and Neymar. Many tipped them to replicate the success of Barcelona's famous MSN and that's why PSG's failure will still sting Pochettino to this day.

The Paris club set their sights on building their own Galacticos instead of focusing on balance. Eventually, it cost Pochettino his job as he failed to win the Champions League.

In more unfortunate fashion, that proved to be the final straw for PSG, who changed their transfer strategy under Luis Enrique and became back-to-back Champions League winners between 2025 and 2026.

With or without success, it should come as no surprise that Pochettino's most-used player during his time in France was Mbappe.

The forward scored 67 goals in 75 games - representing yet another striker who starred under the South American's guidance, with the Frenchman still ranked among the best strikers in world football. He may not be a Champions League winner, but Poch certainly knows how to platform goalscorers. Though it speaks volumes that neither Messi, one of the greatest football players of all time, nor Neymar rank inside the top five for appearances.

Whilst his PSG spell can be summed up by Champions League failure, Pochettino's spell at Chelsea was disappointing for other reasons entirely. The South American decided to enter the turbulance of BlueCo's big-money spending, only to become one of many managers to fall short of expectations amid the chaos.

This time, he didn't fall back on an attacking midfielder or a star striker. Perhaps that's partly why Chelsea failed. Instead, it was the high-energy Conor Gallgher who made the most appearances under Pochettino.

For the first time, it was the manager's midfield that he trusted the most. In other sides, they've taken a more backstage role while the stars do the business going forward.

At Chelsea, however, Gallagher was asked to take control of a failing side, setting the tone of what was supposed to be a high-energy system. To no surprise, it took little time for cracks to appear as Poch lasted just 11 months at Stamford Bridge.

Pochettino's most used players at Chelsea

Alex Freeman is the most surprising entry of the lot in this list. For the first time in his managerial career, Pochettino's most-used player was a defender during his spell in charge of USA. The former Chelsea boss decided to lean on fullback as he got back on track as a coach following a frustrating few years.

Meanwhile, Tim Ream, in his late 30s, played over 20 times for Pochettino, who had no concerns about the American's age. Even at the 2026 World Cup, the former Fulham man took his place amongst the most-trusted men in the squad.

So is that a sign of things to come? As Pochettino evolves, there is a chance that he looks to trust more experienced players and defenders at the start of a project rather than youthful exhuberance or attacking stars. If that is the case, then that should be good news for Man United's veteran defender, Harry Maguire.

What's more, it's also worth noting that Malick Tilman also played a large part. But for a brief blip at Chelsea, Pochettino has turned towards attacking midfielders throughout most of his managerial career. Up next, Bruno Fernandes, one of the best midfielders in the Premier League right now, awaits.

A return to relentless energy and tactical intensity with targeted youth promotion and off-field discipline at Old Trafford.

#1306. If Spanish refs can speak up so can ours... over to you, Willie

Published: 12:39 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 12:46 EST, 13 November 2026

Since the beginning of the month in Spain, referees have started making themselves available for interview after matches to explain decisions and improve transparency.

It has led to people here asking why Scotland’s whistlers aren’t doing the same — and those questions are perfectly valid.

Back in August 2023, leading official John Beaton addressed calls for greater openness around VAR and gave the impression the refereeing firmament were in favour of a new spirit of glasnost.

‘Anything to explain how we are arriving at decisions and anything we can do to show people what we do on a Saturday and what happens in the VAR centre, we absolutely welcome,’ he said.

‘The more transparency, the better. The more questions we get, the more answers we can provide and, we hope, get to a better place,’

That was followed by new head of refereeing Willie Collum’s VAR show on YouTube the following season. At that point, there seemed a real move to lift the lid and build confidence in our men in black. There was talk of Collum doing his programme more than once a month and suggestions referees might even be open to being interviewed post-match in the right circumstances.

Unfortunately, though, all that has come to nothing and last term — in which controversial decisions had a huge effect on the title race — feels like it could become an obstacle in the way of progress.

Head of Referees Willie Collum should be applauded for speaking up on the SFA VAR show

It needn’t be, though. There has always been a feeling among referees that being put in front of the cameras carried danger. SFA Ian Maxwell has also spoken about the game being subject to ‘fairly hysterical commentary’ when something bad happens.

The media environment here is nowhere near as febrile as in Spain, though. It has four newspapers dedicated to sport alone. There are countless chat shows on council telly full of talking heads. Ages ago, news bulletins there had lipreaders telling viewers what coaches and players were saying on the park. Jose Mourinho is also back ruffling officials’ feathers at Real Madrid.

Getting Spanish refs to a place where they feel ready to be interviewed has taken time. It has also taken extra cash for them from TV money and it can still go a lot further.

A selected referee will speak to broadcast rights-holders only. And it’s not after every game. Only selected fixtures.

The SFA made real progress a couple of years back in lifting the curtain and should seek to rediscover that momentum — even though it won’t make the key issue of having to improve overall standards go away.

Since last year, the Spanish FA have been broadcasting their own YouTube show ‘Tiempo de Revision’ to address flashpoints. It should be said that it’s inferior to Collum’s broadcast in terms of content.

It replays incidents against a musical backdrop with captions explaining the decisions. There is no in-game audio, no one like Collum putting himself out there.

Although some of his reasoning for big calls was a bit suspect last term, that programme remains a platform to build from.

There is no reason why referees shouldn’t explain their decision-making after games here. Criticism they may or may not receive in the aftermath shouldn’t come into it.

If Spanish whistlers can go public, so can they.

#1304. New culprit in early Alzheimer’s: blood–brain barrier blocks protective proteins

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Researchers tagged dozens of proteins that can cross the blood-brain barrier and are important for brain health.Credit: K. H. Fung/SPL

For decades, scientists thought of the blood–brain barrier as an impenetrable layer. Over time that view has changed, as researchers realized the barrier was more permeable than first thought. Now, a team have catalogued almost 100 proteins that can pass through it to maintain brain health1.

The team also found that the transport of some of these crucial proteins breaks down in mice with brain diseases that mimic early-stage Alzheimer’s disease.

“The paradigm in the field has been that the blood–brain barrier is normally impermeable and then becomes leaky as a result of Alzheimer’s disease,” says study co-author Andrew Yang, a neuroscientist at Gladstone Institute of Neurological Disease in San Francisco, California. Instead, his team’s work suggests that the blood–brain barrier actively imports proteins that the brain needs to function and the loss of these proteins drives the dysfunction seen early in the disease, he adds.

Yang and his colleagues developed a technique to label a large array of proteins in the blood and track those that can enter the brain. Of the 861 proteins they mapped, 92 crossed the blood–brain barrier into the brain. Most of these proteins were produced in distant organs, particularly the liver.

The team focused on apolipoprotein A1 (APOA1), which has been linked to potential protective effects against Alzheimer’s disease2. Once inside the brain, APOA1 stimulates brain cells called astrocytes to release cholesterol, which is important for maintaining the synapses through which neurons communicate. But how the protein crossed the blood–brain barrier has been unclear until now, says Yang.

His team found that two receptors for APOA1 — SR-B1 and ABCA1 — are present on the blood–brain barrier as well as astrocytes. This suggests how the protein moves from the blood–brain barrier to the specific brain cells that need them, the authors say.

When Yang’s team blocked the ABCA1 receptor in laboratory-grown astrocytes, the protein no longer had the same cholesterol-regulating effects.

Scientists have long known that the blood–brain barrier breaks down as Alzheimer’s advances, letting harmful molecules leak into the brain. Yang’s team found that a different problem emerges first.

Using their labelling technique in a mouse model of Alzheimer’s disease, the researchers found that the blood–brain barrier stopped importing protective proteins such as APOA1 into the brain before the barrier began to break down. This disruption to the protein transport was accompanied by a loss of neuronal connections, behavioural changes and other early hallmarks of the disease.

Yang and the team wondered whether increasing the supply of APOA1 in the blood might help to counter some of the damage caused by Alzheimer’s disease. To find out, the team engineered mice with Alzheimer’s to produce extra APOA1 in the liver. When more APOA1 crossed the blood–brain barrier and entered the brain, the mice showed fewer Alzheimer’s-disease-related markers. For example, they had reduced fat build-up in astrocytes and lower levels of inflammatory molecules.

#1302. Tottenham Can Forget About Will Lankshear By Signing Igor Matanovic

Tottenham Hotspur could look to address their centre-forward issues in January, and one player they are closely observing is Freiburg's Igor Matanovic.

After a turbulent start to the new campaign, Spurs have improved in recent weeks under Roberto De Zerbi, although they remain locked in a congested mid-table in the Premier League. Scoring just ten goals in their opening ten matches, it's clear that the Italian's side's primary issue is their inability to find the back of the net.

Richarlison has effectively been frozen out by the former Brighton boss, after a reported breakdown in the relationship between the player and the coach. Meanwhile, Dominic Solanke has scored just four league goals since the start of last season, and Omar Marmoush only has one strike to his name in a Tottenham shirt.

To add insult to injury, Will Lankshear, who Spurs sold to Middlesbrough in the summer for a fee that could rise to £20 million, is currently the top goalscorer in the Championship. The 21-year-old has 15 goals in 16 appearances across all competitions for Boro.

Lankshear's Statistics 2026/27 (Championship Only)

Letting one of their prized young stars leave before he had time to develop into a prolific goalscorer will be a difficult bullet to bite, but Tottenham's hierarchy could still redeem themselves by signing Matanovic in an upcoming window.

Speaking on GIVEMESPORT's Market Madness podcast, Ben Jacobs revealed that Tottenham are interested in Matanovic, whilst mooting the possibility that the Lilywhites could opt for a short-term solution to their striker problem in January.

"I think they could go for one in January if the right target presents itself," he said.

"It's a shame how the Richarlison situation has panned out. Igor Matanovic is one name, as I exclusively revealed, that Tottenham like. They may look for something a little bit more short-term, like a loan. The same for Manchester United. If they can't find the right target, or maybe someone with a bit more experience within the Premier League, then they can reassess in the summer. What they won't want to do is necessarily go all in and panic buy in January for someone on a long-term contract, instead of just biding their time and waiting it out."

Given Matanovic is only 23 and is reportedly tied down at Freiburg until 2029, he's unlikely to qualify as a 'short-term' solution option. The German club probably aren't keen on sanctioning the departure of their star striker midway through the season unless they receive a substantial offer, and Jacobs' comments suggest that making over-the-odds offers isn't the approach Spurs want to take this winter.

That said, a summer move for Matanovic remains very much on the cards.

Given how well Lankshear has started the season, it's likely that he'll be the subject of interest from Premier League clubs in the summer if Middlesbrough don't achieve promotion. Thus, it's possible that he'll be lining up for an English top-flight side next term, and it probably won't be Tottenham.

This will be a tough pill to swallow for Spurs, who had the prospect in their grasp not long ago. However, Matanovic could prove to be a much better player than Lankshear, and more capable of reaching the level that Spurs aspire to be at than his English counterpart.

The Croatian scored 15 goals across all competitions for Freiburg last term, and he already has eight this time around.

Standing at 6'5", Matanovic is physically and aerially dominant, whilst he provides the Breisgau-Brasilianer with a dependable focal point throughout matches.

Matanovic's Statistics 2026/27 (Bundesliga Only)

He can certainly still become more efficient with his finishing, but his 4.32 shots per 90 minutes is a positive indication that he has plenty more goals within him, which could be unlocked under a manager like De Zerbi.

If a deal for Matanovic is there to be done in the summer at a reasonable price, it's one that the Lilywhites should look to get over the line.

All Statistics via FotMob - correct as of 13/09/2026

#1301. Boston was a lovely holiday romance, but let's leave it there. Talk of taking Tartan Army back there every two years is just cringeworthy

Published: 11:18 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 13:03 EST, 13 November 2026

Boston was the loveliest little holiday romance. An unforgettable moment in time. But let’s just leave it at that, shall we?

Can’t we just allow those involved in the shenanigans around the World Cup last summer to reflect misty-eyed on doorways to Xanadu being opened by the tilt of the kilt and maybe even the heady nights they can’t remember much about at all?

Or does everything have to be milked to the max these days? Flogged like a dead horse to benefit someone or other. Ruined, really. Played out until every scintilla of fun has been drained out of it.

A bit like Yes, Sir, I Can Boogie. That started out as a bona-fide hoot. A half-cut Andy Considine dressing up in drag with his friends and family during his stag do in London in 2015 and making a music video around Baccara’s 1977 hit. It went viral. Obviously. It was – and is – hilarious.

When Scotland’s players resurrected it in the dressing room in Serbia five years later – with Considine as part of the squad – after the national team had ended a 23-year wait to make it to a major competition, it was simply inspired.

Every second of those infectious scenes exuded elation, joy, togetherness and pin-sharp humour, a killer recipe for the interludes that make life and living so great.

Now? Even the opening bars of the song bring on a sense of dread. It was splattered over T-shirts, played everywhere on repeat and still gets aired at every Scotland home game.

The Tartan Army march to Boston's Fenway Park baseball stadium

It’s boring. It’s been done to death and now lives firmly in that grim, stagnant swamp known as Scottish mainstream culture along with munchy boxes, Bitz N Pieces, theatre shows about the Old Firm and ex-footballers suddenly developing a personality and getting involved in stage shows to tell the world how Wee Dazza once did Big Jazza a beauty in the dressing-room by leaving a squelchy banana in his shoe. The banter anawrat.

Everything ends up spoiled here and it looks like we’re already well down that road with the Tartan Army thanks to the news breaking that the Scottish FA are in talks with the State of Massachusetts over a biennial friendly match at the Gillette Stadium, the black hole amid the festivity at the finals thanks to struggling past Haiti and embarrassing ourselves against Morocco.

State senator Paul Feeney has been across the pond to press the flesh. Massachusetts senate president Karen Spilka is already talking about staging Tartan Day – presumably some rip-off of that twee, shortbread-tin abomination in New York – and ‘other events’.

The heart sinks. Listen, the minute politicians get involved in any kind of ‘happening’, the best thing to do is give it a wide berth.

Mind you, before the Big Swerve, it might be worthwhile having someone remind these characters from The Bay State that Massachusetts’ first contribution to Scotland supporters hitting town in summer involved hiking the cost of the 25-mile train ride from Boston to the ground from $20 to a ludicrous $80.

What unfolded there in mid-June was nothing to do with them. It was everything to do with spontaneity. As it ought to be. A glorious coming-together of all sorts of folk up for a right, royal carry-on.

There were so many glorious vignettes. Scotland punters taking over Red Sox games. Bars running out of beer. Mass marches. Local women, doped-up on Outlander, telling TikTok how a bunch of jakeys intent on drinking anything within arm’s reach – except Bud Light, of course – were making them feel ‘seen’.

The Tartan Army make their presence known in Boston during the summer's World Cup

It was brilliant. A short spell in which stars aligned and magic happened. Boston had everything the Tartan Army required. And going by the testimony of Bostonians, the Tartan Army brought badly needed vitality back to the streets of a city quietened by Covid and other factors.

Everybody won. Everyone there still dines out on the memory. But that’s where it should stay. In the memory. These conversations about trying to recapture that spirit, recreate it every two years around some meaningless friendly against opposition unconfirmed and possible business meetings on the periphery, feel quite sad. How can it have any legs long-term?

Joe and Josephine Punter have moved on. They’re on the batter in other places now. Next week, it’s Switzerland for a Nations League game. After that, it’s wherever the draw for the Euro qualifiers throws them. New cities. New adventures. As football away days ought to be. In, out, shake it all about.

Away days are not about teaming up with suit-wearing dignitaries to be paraded at the town hall, like performing seals in plaid – even though there does appear to be an element of the Scotland support that enjoys that kind of thing.

Away days are not about being used as political capital or forming part of some constructed ‘festival’.

Look, in most aspects of life, it’s generally best not to go back. Sticking traffic cones on top of statues all over town won’t be as funny next time. There won’t be a 20,000-strong travelling support spending their life savings on games an entire generation had been waiting for. There won’t be anything like the same buzz, if any.

Some folk might fancy returning once, just to see if it feels the same. The idea that this is going to be a big deal every two years, though, feels deeply misguided.

Boston’s Irish. Not Scottish. That Tartan Week nonsense in New York is a toe-curlingly awful melange of kilts, Scottie dogs and actors living in America telling everyone back home how to vote.

No self-respecting Scot should give it house room. If there is a plan for the same thing in Boston, the same rules apply.

Like NYC, it’ll suit those from the political class in the mood for a junket, of course. John Swinney will already be counting the air miles if there’s another game in Massachusetts to go to.

The public, of course, is still counting the cost of the First Minister’s last trip there for the World Cup. The bill came in at £45,000 for him and two senior aides to fly business class. The entire trip for government staff came to more than £98,000.

Swinney plays the role with aplomb at these affairs, supping a pint in his Scotland top. The Scottish Football Association need to ask themselves this, though: why should they put themselves at the heart of some kind of cock-eyed project to build bridges politically?

The Tartan Army leave their signature traffic cone in a park in Boston

First up, the players are hardly likely to welcome a pointless week in America being added to a jam-packed schedule. More importantly, though, what exactly has this SNP-led administration, outwith giving a few bob to grassroots, done for Scottish football down the years?

From this vantage point, they’ve been no friend to the national game or its followers. The Offensive Behaviour at Football Act, repealed in 2018, was a scandalous piece of legislation that criminalised fans and made going to football unpleasant.

Clubs have had to fight tooth and nail to secure trials to sell pints inside stadiums when other sports are allowed to do what they like. After trouble in Glasgow city centre ahead of the Old Firm League Cup final two years ago, Swinney stated that ‘the clubs have got a responsibility to make sure their fans behave properly’.

Inside their grounds, yes. What are they meant to do, though, about teenagers running amok on Argyle Street?

Looking after that is the job of the police. Of course, anyone reading 1919 magazine, funded by the Scottish Police Federation, earlier this year will have noted an article about policing around football being ‘chaotic’ and understaffed because of SNP Government budget cuts.

Just like everything else in this sorry little nation built on buying votes for ‘free stuff’, Police Scotland is creaking at the seams. Why would anyone want to get involved in another transatlantic piece of theatre selling some false, outdated, vaguely comical vision of it to foreigners?

A pointless Scotland friendly – served up as part of some forced, hackneyed ‘cultural exchange’ or not – is hardly an idea to be getting on board with.

Pure dead brilliant, it won’t be. More like pure cringe.

#1300. Gary Lineker Predicts How Long Pochettino Will Last as Man Utd Manager

Manchester United have agreed a two-and-a-half year deal to appoint Mauricio Pochettino as the club's new manager, with the announcement coming on Friday, and Gary Lineker has already predicted how long the Argentine will last at the club.

Man United finally relieved Michael Carrick of his duties on Thursday morning even though his dismissal had been publicly mooted in the media since Monday.

Jason Wilcox and Omar Berrada travelled to Monaco for talks with co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe over the 45-year-old's future, with the recommendation that he should be sacked and replaced by Pochettino.

The Red Devils have been working on an agreement to bring the former Tottenham Hotspur boss to Old Trafford this week, with GIVEMESPORT sources revealing on Wednesday night that they had reached an agreement in principle with the 54-year-old over personal terms.

Pochettino is set to take charge of the United States' two fixtures against Haiti within the next week, before heading to Manchester to prepare for the trip to Anfield to face Liverpool a week on Sunday.

After Sir Alex Ferguson managed United for 27 years between 1986 and 2013, the departure of Carrick means that Pochettino will be the 13th managerial appointment the club has made since the icon's departure 13 years ago, including interim hires.

The odds are stacked against Pochettino having a long reign at Old Trafford and, speaking on the latest episode of the Rest is Football podcast, Lineker doesn't believe he will get close to lasting the entirety of his 30-month deal.

The former Match of the Day host said: "I look at that club, and I don't think it.... I see Pochettino going in there, and I think they'll probably get off to a reasonable start. They'll do okay for a while.

I think for Pochettino, it's a big club, Manchester United, big by name. He'll go in there, and then he'll be disappointed with the way things occur in the future. And if he's still there in 18 months, I'll be surprised, because again and again, rinse and repeat.

"The scapegoat is always the coach, and you can see that. And I think the real problems are above the coach."

In recent years, the likes of Erik ten Hag, Ruben Amorim and even Carrick, following his success last season, may have expected a good length of time in charge at Old Trafford.

Carrick's permanent position is gone within weeks, while Amorim only lasted just over a year in charge.

Given United currently lie in the relegation places in the Premier League, it is clear that the pressure will instantly be on Pochettino to produce performances and results.

He may well be able to do that, but the fact that he will be the 13th appointment since Sir Alex left 13 years ago tells you all you need to know that there are bigger issues at the club than simply the manager.

Firstly, the players must take some accountability because they are performing nowhere near the levels they were in the first half of 2026, and this has been an ongoing issue under previous managers too.

The recruitment team of Wilcox and Berrada must take some blame too, given the say they have over who the manager is and which players are being brought to the club.

In a summer when United needed to get it right ahead of returning to the Champions League, they spent £70m on an injured player who has only recently started appearing, while the £50m fee for Andrey Santos is looking more baffling by the day.

Ratcliffe has hardly made a positive impact in general too, while the view of supporters on the Glazers has been clear for a very long time.

United have a lot of issues right now and it would be no surprise if Lineker is correct, and Pochettino is no longer the club's manager by the end of next season.

Mauricio Pochettino is set to be named as Michael Carrick's replacement at Old Trafford

#1299. Agent: ‘Pio Esposito future is certainly at Inter’ despite Arsenal and Man Utd focus

Pio Esposito is targeted by clubs including Arsenal and Manchester United, but the Italy star’s agent assures ‘his future is at Inter, without doubt, for many years.’

The 21-year-old bagged a brace in last night’s 3-1 Nations League victory over France at San Siro, taking his total tally to nine goals in just 14 senior caps.

It further raised his profile, having already attracted interest from the Premier League, with giants like Arsenal and Manchester United ready to spend big money.

However, his agent warns they can forget about tempting the striker away from the Stadio Meazza.

“His future is at Inter, without doubt,” representative Mario Giuffredi told Radio Napoli Centrale.

“Pio grew up at Inter, he is very happy in Milan. The club has always shown a sense of belonging and gratitude, they never held back. He will certainly remain at Inter for many years.”

A product of the Nerazzurri youth academy along with big brother Sebastiano, Pio had gone out on loan in Serie B to Spezia and was expecting another temporary move, until Cristian Chivu took over and decided to bet on him straight away.

Things could’ve been very different, as his agent confirms Napoli made an approach when Pio Esposito was still at Spezia.

“It is true, President Aurelio De Laurentiis has always shown an interest in the player, but also his brother Sebastiano. Sometimes you just don’t have the right conditions to do deals, but Pio never thought about leaving, because he is very happy at Inter.

“The Nerazzurri jersey is like his second skin.”

It was a special night for the Esposito family at San Siro, because while Pio scored twice, Sebastiano missed a penalty against France.

“I must admit, I didn’t watch either of the two penalties, it was too nerve-wracking,” confessed their agent.

“I was having dinner with their brother, Salvatore, and we stepped away from the TV. Pio felt the responsibility after his missed penalty against Bosnia, so scoring last night was like taking that weight off his mind.”

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of this Europa League tie between Bournemouth and AC Milan at the Vitality Stadium.

Back in 2008, Bournemouth’s prospect of a European meeting with Milan seemed impossible. After entering administration with crippling debts of around £4m, Bournemouth were handed a 10-point deduction and relegated from League One. To make matters worse, a hefty 17-point deduction was given to the club ahead of the 2008-09 League Two season, with relegation to non-league seeming inevitable. However, midway through the campaign, the transformative Eddie Howe was parachuted in as Bournemouth’s saviour, eventually guiding the club to safety.

Fast forward to October 2026 in an extraordinary rise and Bournemouth are competing in their first-ever European campaign in the club’s 127-year existence. They welcome Milan to Dorset, having earned back-to-back victories over Real Sociedad and Sturm Graz to kick off their inaugural Europa League adventure in style.

Now, they host the second most successful side in the European Cup history. In terms of heritage and silverware, these clubs could not be further apart, but on the pitch, it’s incredibly tough to call.

On Sunday, Marco Rose’s Bournemouth picked up their first Premier League win of the season, beating 10-man Sunderland 2-0 at the Vitality thanks to goals from Marcus Tavernier and Evanilson to move out of the relegation zone.

Meanwhile, Ruben Amorim is in charge at Milan and returns to England after a tumultuous 14-month reign at Manchester United, where he was sacked in January. Milan lost their opening Europa League fixture 2-0 at home to Benfica, before battering Salzburg 4-0 in Austria, with Alphadjo Cisse netting a stunning hat-trick.

Crystal Palace are also in the Europa League tonight and face an incredibly daunting away trip to Turkish side Besiktas. Pressure is firmly on manager Pierre Sage following the 5-0 humiliation against Brighton last weekend and a shaky start to the season. Palace lost 3-2 to Sage’s former employers Lyon in their previous Europa League outing, with a positive performance and result needed to restore the fans’ faith.

Both games kick-off at 20:00, with team news coming imminently.

#1297. Raum or Robinson: Pochettino's First Man Utd Signing Has Just Become Clear

The Mauricio Pochettino era at Manchester United has officially begun, and the former Chelsea and Tottenham manager will undoubtedly already be looking at how he can improve his squad in the upcoming January transfer window.

The Red Devils find themselves in a precarious position in the Premier League table; they sit 18th, having won just one of their opening ten matches. This dire form is what prompted the Old Trafford hierarchy to make a change in the dugout, dismissing Michael Carrick and appointing Pochettino as the former midfielder's successor.

The Argentine's tenure will commence in practice after the international break when his team visit Anfield, but the work will no doubt start immediately.

The new manager will be devising transfer plans alongside his higher-ups, mapping out ways in which they can bolster the club's roster this winter.

A key area that needs addressing, and could be addressed in January, is left-back, which has been a problem position for United so far this season.

The perennially-injured Luke Shaw miraculously featured in all 38 of Manchester United's Premier League matches last season. Given his fitness record, this clean bill of health was unlikely to continue into the new campaign with the addition of Champions League matches, and unsurprisingly, it hasn't.

The England international has been unavailable since October 10th, and United have subsequently been forced to resort to using Diogo Dalot on his weaker side, which hasn't gone well. This is because they failed to sign a competitor for Shaw over the summer, despite courting Newcastle United's Lewis Hall for several months.

The Red Devils' recruitment team decided not to pull the trigger on any of their left-back targets, and instead hold fire until a later date. After seeing how costly this decision has been to their team so far this campaign, they may look to rectify this error in January.

Speaking on GIVEMESPORT's Market Madness Podcast, Ben Jacobs revealed that this is certainly a possibility, while naming two left-sided defenders United have been linked with in the past.

"There's still a chance that with Man United we see a left-back," he said.

"They've looked at David Raum in the past. Antonee Robinson might be a player that a few clubs look at in the winter market, especially if it looks like Fulham are struggling, and there may be some opportunism there, so we will get some winter movement. But there are just two bits of caution. The first is that this inflated market from the summer may bleed over into the winter and put a lot of clubs off spending mid-season. And the second broader point is that the winter market is always a seller's market, not a buyer's market. So it is a lot harder to get the business done."

Jacobs' words of caution suggest a move for Hall might be off the table in January. Newcastle are unlikely to sanction the departure of one of their most important players midway through the season, particularly to a rival.

However, a more modest move for either David Raum or Antonee Robinson certainly feels plausible.

Clearly, signing a left-back should be the priority for United in January. While centre-back and striker are other pressing areas of concern, Pochettino at least has options in these positions. At left-back, it's just Shaw, and perhaps Patrick Dorgu, although the Dane has looked more comfortable further forward in his time in Manchester.

Raum has been a dependable attacking left-back in the Bundesliga for several years now, and would certainly be an adept addition for United to make. That said, there have always been some question marks around his defensive acumen, which is likely the reason behind his inability to secure a move to a top European club.

Statistical Comparison 205/25 (League Only)

Meanwhile, Robinson has proven himself in the Premier League over a number of years, both as an offensive outlet and as a reliable defender. He is consistently one of the quickest players in the English top flight, and has established himself as one of the best in his position in the division.

On top of this, as Jacobs alluded to, the American could present United with an opportunistic move if he pushes for an exit from Craven Cottage.

Pochettino will be the new Manchester United manager after Michael Carrick was sacked

Fulham are struggling this season, and this could provide Robinson with leverage in the transfer market, with the West Londoners unlikely to hold one of their longest-serving players hostage, particularly given that his contract expires in 18 months.

It's a no-brainer who Pochettino's first signing should be at Manchester United.

#1296. Tare: ‘Leao priority was not football, Liverpool had Gomez agreement’

Former Milan director Igli Tare reveals ‘football was no longer a priority’ for Rafael Leao before he joined Galatasaray, while Liverpool ‘pulled out’ of a deal for Joe Gomez.

Tare was at the club for the 2025/26 campaign, but then fired in May along with coach Max Allegri, CEO Giorgio Furlani and director Geoffrey Moncada for failing to secure a Champions League spot.

It was already becoming apparent that Leao would not be staying on, as his contract was due to run down in June 2028, and the Rossoneri were not prepared to offer him a new deal at those wages.

“I had only known of Leao from the outside, but when I got the opportunity to get to know him in person, I thought he was an extraordinary guy,” Tare told the Sky Sport Italia Calcio Unplugged podcast.

“I really cared for him very much as a person. However, he was the player we all expected more from. I think football was no longer a priority for him. That’s how to read the situation.”

Leao continues to balance his playing career with his role as a musician, releasing a rap album last year.

“I think he was focused more on his life outside of football, so music, fashion, things like that. I never doubted his love for Milan, you could tell he suffered at not performing consistently, he had a lot of fitness problems, so always had the handbrake on.

“I tried to have more individual meetings with him than any other Milan player, and every time I got the sense he wanted to do more. But wanting to is sometimes not enough.”

It took a long time for the Rossoneri and Leao to find a buyer, eventually settling for Galatasaray late into the transfer window, so could he have been sold in 2025?

“No concrete offers ever arrived for him,” revealed Tare.

Meanwhile, Tare also discussed the somewhat chaotic transfer strategy over the summer of 2025, when coach Max Allegri forced a rethink.

“It was difficult for us because we decided to change system five days before the end of the transfer window,” explained the former director of sport.

“Going from a 4-3-3 to a three-man defence made it hard for us to find someone of that level in five days.

“We were a bit unlucky, first because Manuel Akanji went to Inter as we weren’t in the Champions League, then we had an agreement with Liverpool for Joe Gomez. However, when Marc Guehi’s move from Crystal Palace to Liverpool collapsed at the last minute, Liverpool pulled out.

“We had been waiting only for that move for us to sign the paperwork. In order to avoid being without centre-backs, we signed Odogu at the last minute as a signing for the future.”
